transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
Tomorrow is the first Monday in October,
which marks the traditional start
of the new Supreme Court term.
Immigration, climate change, and more are on the docket,
including a case that asks whether it is unconstitutional
to ban semi-automatic assault-style weapons.
NPR's Nina Totenberg reports.
>> On the one hand, for instance,
the AR-15 rifle can deliver up to 100 bullets per minute
without any enhancements.
On the other hand, there are some 16 million
semi-automatic weapons in the U.S., and it's unclear,
for instance, how a ban would work
without taking weapons away from law-abiding citizens.
There are many other controversies facing the court,
everything from test cases on public funding
for religious schools, lengthy detention
of immigrants without a hearing,
and, of course, very likely questions
about the conduct of elections.
Nina Totenberg, NPR News, Washington.
>> There's less than a month to go
before the 2026 midterm elections.
And NPR's Domenico Montanaro says the political landscape
appears to be shifting more in the Democrats' favor.
>> History isn't kind to the President's party
in midterm elections, and this year is shaping
up to be no different.
Negative views of the economy and the Iran War
have created a tough environment for swing-district Republicans.
Democrats are the favorites to pick up control of the House,
and the Senate appears to be within reach.
That isn't something that was thought possible
at the beginning of the cycle.
But while Democrats are in the driver's seat,
there are lots of reasons for why their gains may be limited.
Redistricting has helped insulate Republicans to an extent.
Most of the districts that are competitive
are in places Trump won in 2024,
and the Democratic Party remains unpopular.
>> Domenico Montanaro, NPR News, Washington.
>> Israeli investigators believe that the co-pilot
who attacked the captain of a plane flying from Dubai
to Tel Aviv in midair last week likely acted alone.
That's according to a person familiar with the matter,
but not authorized to speak publicly.
NPR's Kat Lonsdorf reports from Tel Aviv.
>> The Israeli investigation into the attack
is pointing toward the likelihood
that the co-pilot was a lone wolf attacker,
that source told NPR.
Investigators in the United Arab Emirates,
which is leading the inquiry working with Israeli officials,
announced they have deemed the incident
an attempted terrorist attack,
although the motive is still unknown.
The co-pilot is from Oman, according to Israeli officials,
raising questions about how he was allowed
to fly a plane heading to Israel,
as Israel does not allow pilots from countries
it doesn't have diplomatic relations with
to fly in its airspace.
Several lawmakers in Israel are demanding an investigation
into security failures that could have led to the incident.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
>> German Chancellor Friedrich Merz
made a surprise visit to Kyiv today,
where he announced new aid package for Ukraine.
It's worth over $1.5 billion.
You're listening to NPR News.
"Avengers Endgame" has reclaimed the number one spot
on Hollywood's all-time worldwide box office chart
this weekend.
NPR's Bob Mondello has details.
>> "Marvel's superhero epic" first became the highest-grossing
film in history back in 2019, passing "Avatar,"
which had held that title for 10 years.
>> "Avengers! Assemble."
>> Then the original "Avatar" was re-released in 2022
to promote a sequel and earned enough to reclaim the top spot.
>> Marine in an Avatar body. That's a potent mix.
>> Now it's "Avengers" that has a sequel coming,
so following the same playbook,
"Endgame" has been re-released and has retaken the title.
It's a friendly competition.
Both films are Disney releases,
and their jockeying reflects rising prices
more than attendance.
In terms of tickets sold,
neither film comes close to...
>> I'm the king of the world!
>> "Titanic," Bob Mondello, NPR News.
>> It has taken decades of negotiations with Greece,
but the remains of a medieval ruler
have finally been returned to Bulgaria.
The remains of Czar Samuel were discovered 60 years ago
and flown to Sofia, where they were taken to the church
of St. Sophia, where Samuel was baptized.
Czar Samuel was a warrior emperor
who fought the Byzantine Empire
and has been a symbol of Bulgaria's national identity.
Greek and Bulgarian leaders attended the ceremony
marking the handing over of the remains.
They emphasized both unity and cooperation
between the two nations.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Supreme Court term begins with cases on assault weapons, religious school funding, and election conduct
Democrats favored to gain House control in 2026 midterms as political landscape shifts in their favor
Israeli investigators believe co-pilot who attacked plane captain from Dubai to Tel Aviv acted alone
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visits Kyiv, announces over $1.5 billion new aid package for Ukraine
Avengers Endgame reclaims number one spot on all-time worldwide box office chart after re-release
Remains of medieval Czar Samuel returned to Bulgaria after decades of negotiations with Greece
